newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rival leaders jovial as Cyprus talks start.
newsitem.headline: Rival leaders jovial as Cyprus talks start.

text.p: Leaders of the two main communities involved in the 34-year-old Cyprus problem put on a display of joviality on Monday as they met for the formal opening of a new round of talks.
But diplomats analysing comments made by both sides in advance of the talks and the current situation on the island said prospects for movement towards a solution looked dim.

Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, clad in dark suits, appeared relaxed and joked with each other in front of reporters as they and their teams sat down for the discussions at a luxury Swiss hotel.
Around the green-baize table with them was United Nations special envoy for Cyprus Diego Cordovez, a former foreign minister of Ecuador, who is chairing the week-long encounter.
Neither spoke to reporters but Denktash adviser Ergun Olgun told Reuters: "We're here to keep the talks going."

Gloom was deepened in advance of the meeting by Denktash who, after arriving in Switzerland on Sunday, insisted on absolute political equality with the 78-year-old Clerides -- anathema to the Greek Cypriots.

"There really seems little chance of any sort of breakthrough," said one envoy close to the talks, being held amid high security and a media blackout in the village of Glion overlooking Montreux and Lake Geneva.
The discussions follow a first round last month at Troutbeck, near New York, which appeared to make no headway.

The 73-year-old Denktash, head of the breakaway northern Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday the talks could proceed only on the basis of political equality on paper and in effect.
He called on Cordovez to agree to a new track in the negotiations on the basis of equality. "We have come with goodwill to defend what is ours," Denktash said during a stopover in Geneva.

"The attempt to set up a federal partnership failed so far because a federal partnership can only be established between two equals. That equality has been destroyed by the world by treating the Greek Cypriot partner as the government of all."

Public positions have become more entrenched since Troutbeck. Stakes are also higher as Cyprus prepares for entry talks with the European Union next year and Turkey says it will move towards partial integration with the north.
But Clerides himself made no press statement on arrival in Switzerland, heading straight for Glion.

Denktash accused the EU of getting in the way of a deal and threatened to pull out of the negotiations: "If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," he said.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence.
They have been separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia, backed by the junta then ruling Greece.
